sections.html:
• Common name: Spotted sand catlet

This species, along with a few others, was placed in the genus Leptoglanis but was reclassified following the work of Mo (1991), Diogo (2003b) and Roberts (2003). There are still a few undescribed species.

Africa: Cunene, Okavango and Zambezi, Pungwe, Buse and Save basins, and Lake Malawi basin, Lake Rukwa basin. Type locality: In Bubu near Kondoa/Irangi.

Zaireichthys rotundiceps was previously regarded as a species complex and its exact distribution needs to be determined. It has been reported from the Democratic Republic of Congo to Kenya, and south to South Africa, but it might only be present in Tanzania. More information on the distribution, current status, ecology, uses and possible threats is needed for an accurate assessment of the risk of extinction of this species. This dwarf amphiliid catfish is therefore listed as Data Deficient (IUCN 2016).
Inhabits fairly shallow water. Occurs over sand, usually buried with just the eyes protruding.
Provide an aquarium with a sand substrate with a number of rocks in the rear of the tank. Smaller fish such as tetras can be added for the upper layers.
Eggs are few (12–16) and large (3–5 mm diameter), suggesting possible parental care.

Description: Dorsal spines (total): 2; dorsal soft rays (total): 5–6; anal spines: 0; anal soft rays: 11–13; vertebrae: 35–38.

This species differs from Zaireichthys lacustris and Z. maravensis in possessing a premaxillary tooth patch that is less than 40% of the mouth width; it has shorter barbels than Z. wamiensis, maxillary barbel 0.9–1.3 in head length vs. 0.7–0.9; and it is distinguished from Z. compactus by higher number of branched pectoral-fin rays, 7 vs. 6.

Etymology: The genus name Zaireichthys means a fish from Zaire. The specific name rotundiceps: rotundus, rounded; ceps, head, referring to the semi-circular shape of the head when seen from above.

Remarks: As it currently stands, this species probably represents a complex of several different species.
